From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from our playbook, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Executive view

The Seller draft departs materially from the Buyer playbook. The most serious departures concern liability limits, title/fundamental claims, fraud, disclosure and knowledge, Bluefen consent, Riverlark releases, and omitted employee bonus liabilities.

The statement that these matters were “settled at principal level” should not be accepted. In particular, the proposed 20% cap and 18-month period are Buyer fallbacks requiring Amelia Frost’s prior written authority identifying this draft. No such authority has been given. “FINAL” labels and assertions about market practice do not alter our mandate.

## Material departures and pushback

### 1. General warranty cap

**Seller position:** AUD 4.8 million, being 20% of price.

**Playbook:** AUD 6 million, being 25%. The 20% fallback requires Amelia Frost’s prior written authority, which is absent.

**Pushback:** Reinstate a 25% cap. Do not treat 20% as agreed or available for negotiation unless the required written authority is subsequently obtained.

The cap must apply only to the defined general warranty category—not to title, tax, specific indemnities, payment obligations, completion covenants, fraud or other deliberately separate regimes.

---

### 2. De minimis and basket

| Item | Seller draft | Buyer position |
|---|---:|---:|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 |
| Aggregate basket | AUD 250,000 | AUD 50,000 |
| Recovery once exceeded | Only excess | From first dollar |

The Seller’s basket is more than 1% of the price and five times our permitted basket. Combined with the increased de minimis and deductible structure, it would eliminate a significant range of valid claims.

**Pushback:** AUD 5,000 de minimis, AUD 50,000 tipping basket, with recovery from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Aggregation should apply to related claims so a systemic issue cannot be divided into multiple sub-threshold claims.

---

### 3. General claim period

**Seller position:** 18 months.

**Playbook:** 24 months. Eighteen months is an unauthorised fallback requiring Amelia Frost’s prior written approval.

**Pushback:** Reinstate 24 months. A claim properly notified within that period should survive expiry, subject only to an appropriately negotiated period for commencing proceedings.

Reject the Seller’s proposal that a limitation stated for “Claims” applies across every claim category unless expressly excluded. Each category should state its own limits.

---

### 4. Fundamental, title and capacity claims

The Seller proposes to place title and capacity warranties under the general cap, general time period and presumably the general thresholds and knowledge limitations. This is unacceptable.

**Required regime:**

- 100% of the purchase price;
- at least six years;
- outside the general de minimis and basket;
- not defeated by Buyer knowledge or deemed disclosure; and
- not overridden by a generally defined “Claim” limitation.

This is a purchase of 100% of the shares. Failure of title, authority or capacity is qualitatively different from an ordinary business warranty breach.

---

### 5. Fraud and deliberate conduct

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 apparently extend caps, time bars, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to “all Claims of any nature.” No adequate misconduct carve-out is identified.

**Pushback:** Expressly carve out, to the maximum extent enforceable:

- fraud;
- wilful concealment; and
- deliberate misconduct.

The carve-out must apply across all caps, baskets, de minimis thresholds, time limits, exclusive-remedy provisions and non-reliance language. This position cannot be waived.

The definition of “Claim” should also be narrowed so that general warranty limitations do not inadvertently govern tax, title, IP indemnities, debt/payment obligations, completion covenants, specific performance or other separately negotiated rights.

---

### 6. General disclosure and deemed disclosure

Paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 purport to disclose the entire data room, statutory registers and all publicly searchable corporate records. This is directly inconsistent with the playbook.

**Pushback:**

- Delete whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure.
- Require specific, fair disclosure against the relevant warranty.
- A disclosure should contain sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter and permit the Buyer reasonably to understand its likely consequences.
- Mere availability of a document, cross-reference to an index or matter discoverable through a search should not qualify a warranty.

The specific factual entries can be assessed individually, but they should not operate as a blanket release. Paragraph 1.4 may reserve admissions, but it cannot prevent objectively disclosed facts from engaging a warranty, condition, covenant or indemnity.

The data-room cut-off is **22 September 2026**. The Seller should provide an updated index, disclose changes since that date and give signing and Completion bring-downs.

---

### 7. Buyer knowledge

The proposed exclusion covers knowledge of the Buyer and all its advisers, as well as matters merely discoverable in the data room or public records. This is an overly broad actual and constructive knowledge bar.

**Pushback:** Delete clause 8.3 in this form. In particular:

- no deemed or constructive knowledge;
- no imputation of knowledge from the Buyer’s entire adviser group;
- no “discoverable on search” test; and
- no knowledge bar for title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities.

If business warranties are qualified by Seller knowledge, the agreement should identify named Seller knowledge persons and require reasonable enquiry. A Seller knowledge qualifier should not become a disguised Buyer due-diligence risk allocation.

---

### 8. Bluefen consent

Bluefen accounts for approximately AUD 3.6 million of FY26 revenue, or around 30%. The disclosure confirms that neither final consent nor evidence of satisfaction of its conditions is available.

The Seller proposal—reasonable endeavours and satisfaction upon delivery of written consent—is insufficient. Delivery does not establish that the consent is effective or that clause 11.3 conditions have been satisfied.

**Pushback:** Make the following a Buyer-benefit condition precedent:

1. effective written consent in an agreed or satisfactory form;
2. evidence that all associated conditions have been satisfied or validly waived;
3. confirmation that the consent remains effective at Completion; and
4. no material adverse amendment, fee, waiver, termination right or other condition attached to it.

The condition should not be automatically satisfied merely by document delivery. Any waiver should be at the Buyer’s discretion.

---

### 9. Riverlark repayment and security releases

The facility is approximately AUD 3.2 million, but there is no current payout figure, repayment or final security discharge. A release “following Completion” conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free transaction basis and leaves the acquired company exposed to lender security.

**Pushback:**

- obtain a current payout letter through the proposed Completion date;
- repay Riverlark directly from Completion funds;
- obtain effective releases and discharges of all security at Completion;
- verify all relevant PPSR and other security releases; and
- reflect the exact payout in the funds flow.

A post-Completion release is not acceptable. It could only be considered with an irrevocable and enforceable bank undertaking and Amelia Frost’s approval; neither presently exists.

---

### 10. Employee completion bonuses

DD-005 records AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses. They are omitted from the funds flow, and the disclosure does not address payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs.

Saying that the bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” is not enough if the legal or economic liability remains with the Company after Completion.

**Pushback:**

- quantify the bonuses and all associated on-costs;
- confirm who is legally liable and when each amount becomes payable;
- include the full amount as an express funds-flow line item; and
- require Seller funding or an equivalent price adjustment/retention that prevents the Buyer from bearing the liability.

The agreement should also allocate responsibility for any later claim that the calculated on-costs were understated.

---

### 11. Ironquay IP

The proposed indemnity is limited to the specific SOW3 payment. That does not adequately address the underlying risk: title to or transfer of Project Materials may depend on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee.

The AUD 180,000 figure is not independently verified, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Pushback:**

- obtain an up-to-date statement or other independent confirmation of all SOW3 amounts;
- require payment through the Completion mechanics where necessary;
- obtain confirmation of cleared funds and an effective assignment or acknowledgement of ownership;
- preserve the contractual SOW3 cure; and
- broaden the indemnity to cover failure of title or transfer, third-party claims, remediation costs and losses arising from unpaid or disputed SOW3 amounts.

The Ironquay-specific indemnity should not be silently subjected to the general warranty regime. The wider IP regime remains open; we should not accept that it has been settled, nor assume that IP liability will be unlimited.

---

### 12. Export/privacy incident

The Seller’s description of this as an immaterial “preliminary operational matter” is premature. Equally, the documents do not establish access, a confirmed breach, notification duty, harm or any loss amount.

**Pushback should be evidence-led:**

- preserve all relevant logs, messages, access records and forensic material;
- continue the investigation using appropriate technical and legal resources;
- provide regular updates and all material findings;
- establish whether the link was accessed, by whom, when, and what data was exposed;
- document containment, deletion or access-revocation steps;
- assess notification obligations without prejudging the outcome; and
- require a Completion update and ongoing cooperation covenant.

The disclosure should not broadly qualify warranties beyond the specific facts fairly disclosed. At present, there should be no arbitrary price deduction or numeric claim in either direction. Depending on the investigation, a specific indemnity or holdback may need to be considered.

---

### 13. Sandbar supplier renewals

The Seller calls the AUD 330,000 renewals ordinary-course operating costs, but its own disclosure does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or actually ordinary course.

**Pushback:** Obtain and assess:

- executed contracts and renewal notices;
- commencement and payment dates;
- termination rights;
- whether services relate to pre- or post-Completion periods;
- accounting treatment and accruals; and
- whether the renewals were entered into consistently with past practice.

Do not automatically classify the AUD 330,000 as Debt or deduct it from the price. Its treatment should follow the evidence and agreed price mechanics.

---

### 14. Title evidence

DD-012 is a Company-maintained internal share register. It is an important source but not independent proof that the Seller has good, unencumbered title or full authority to transfer the shares.

**Pushback:** Require independent and corroborating evidence, including as applicable:

- constitutional and corporate records;
- original share certificates or an agreed lost-certificate process;
- historical issue and transfer documentation;
- board and shareholder approvals;
- confirmation of legal and beneficial ownership;
- PPSR and other encumbrance searches;
- evidence that no option, trust, security interest or third-party right exists; and
- duly executed transfer and Completion documents.

This evidence is additional to, not a substitute for, the separate fundamental warranty regime.

---

### 15. Tax and general IP provisions remain open

The Seller cannot deem tax and IP “settled under the general regime.” The playbook expressly treats those categories as open.

**Pushback:** Continue negotiating separate and clearly identified tax and IP provisions. We should neither accept the Seller’s general limits automatically nor assume unlimited liability. Any caps, thresholds and survival periods must be expressly negotiated for those categories.

---

### 16. Office lease and Mossvale

The present disclosure does not establish that landlord or Mossvale consent is required merely because of the share sale.

Recommended approach:

- verify the complete relevant clauses and any cross-referenced provisions;
- require compliance with the office lease notification obligation;
- confirm that no change-of-control provision is engaged; and
- do not demand a Mossvale consent solely because its contract restricts assignment, unless the full agreement shows a change-of-control or equivalent trigger.

These matters should not distract from the genuine Bluefen consent issue.

## Recommended negotiation position

1. Reject any claim that the Seller’s marked “FINAL” positions are agreed.
2. Restore the **25% general warranty cap**, **AUD 5,000 de minimis**, **AUD 50,000 tipping basket**, and **24-month** general claims period.
3. Establish a separate **100% / minimum six-year** title, capacity and fundamental regime.
4. Add the mandatory fraud, wilful-concealment and deliberate-misconduct carve-out across every limitation and reliance provision.
5. Delete blanket data-room/public-register disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge.
6. Make effective Bluefen consent, including satisfaction of its conditions, a genuine Completion condition.
7. Require Riverlark repayment and effective security releases through the Completion funds flow.
8. Specifically fund or deduct the AUD 420,000 bonuses plus all on-costs.
9. Broaden the Ironquay protection and independently verify payment and IP transfer.
10. Preserve evidence and complete the export/privacy investigation without assuming a confirmed breach or loss.
11. Investigate Sandbar before deciding its price-mechanics treatment.
12. Require independent title and encumbrance verification.
13. Keep title, tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment obligations and covenants outside any hidden general-claims override.

### 14. Title evidence

DD-012 is a Company-maintained internal share register. It is an important source but not independent proof that the Seller has good, unencumbered title or full authority to transfer the shares.

**Pushback:** Require independent and corroborating evidence, including as applicable:

- constitutional and corporate records;
- original share certificates or an agreed lost-certificate process;
- historical issue and transfer documentation;
- board and shareholder approvals;
- confirmation of legal and beneficial ownership;
- PPSR and other encumbrance searches;
- evidence that no option, trust, security interest or third-party right exists; and
- duly executed transfer and Completion documents.

This evidence is additional to, not a substitute for, the separate fundamental warranty regime.

### 15. Tax and general IP provisions remain open

The Seller cannot deem tax and IP “settled under the general regime.” The playbook expressly treats those categories as open.

**Pushback:** Continue negotiating separate and clearly identified tax and IP provisions. We should neither accept the Seller’s general limits automatically nor assume unlimited liability. Any caps, thresholds and survival periods must be expressly negotiated for those categories.

### 16. Office lease and Mossvale

The present disclosure does not establish that landlord or Mossvale consent is required merely because of the share sale.

Recommended approach:

- confirm that no change-of-control provision is engaged; and
- do not demand a Mossvale consent solely because its contract restricts assignment, unless the full agreement shows a change-of-control or equivalent trigger.

These matters should not distract from the genuine Bluefen consent issue.
